Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs.
  • The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board.
  • “E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs. The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.

The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.

“E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.

According to recent reports, performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.

Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.

The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.

In a recent development, the bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, the token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.

According to recent reports, also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.

According to recent reports, the P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.

The Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.

The Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.

In a recent development, going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.

Sources indicate that as for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.

There’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A woman has revealed that she completed seven marathons in 2026 despite being pregnant for a few of them, admitting that it was a bit “bizarre” at times.

For a lot of people, running a marathon is a goal that they work towards for months, if not years. Some want to set an impressive time, while others just want to be able to say they’ve completed the 26.2 miles.

In the case of Deirdre Keane, the 38-year-old is a seasoned long-distance runner, completing more than 60 marathons to this point. However, throughout 2026, she has been running marathons with an additional hurdle to deal with: she has been pregnant throughout.

“I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” she told the Associated Press, admitting it is a “very unusual” challenge, but noted that she isn’t the first woman to do so.

As per the AP, the 38-year-old had signed up for 11 races in 2026, including the seven major marathons: Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, New York, Sydney and Tokyo.

According to recent reports, “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother,” Keane added. However, she didn’t discover she was pregnant until after running the Tokyo marathon, when she noticed her pace had started to slip.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at New York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane added. “Plus, I got lucky; I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”.

Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal.
  • According to recent reports, videos of the attack demonstrated Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge.
  • With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal. The attack, which led to the partial collapse of the bridge, was significant for a number of reasons. The bridge is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most symbolic assets due to its linking of the occupied Crimean Peninsula and Russia. But perhaps more importantly, the attack's use of Ukrainian connectivity technology highlights the country's lessening of its reliance on Starlink. The modems were crucial to the success of the mission, with the FT reporting that they kept missiles connected to their pilots while they manoeuvred through Russia's air defenses.

According to recent reports, videos of the attack demonstrated Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge. Flamingo missiles are capable of traveling at around 590 miles per hour, requiring a stable and reliable video feed. It's reported that the Ukrainians deliberately chose not to use Starshield, the military version of Musk's Starlink, for the operation, with the company's satellite network having been restricted in recent weeks. That restricted service would have been insufficient for the Crimean Bridge attack, forcing Ukrainian forces to find another solution. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that he has not been told why Starlink's connection has been throttled, with neither the White House nor the Pentagon being forthcoming. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, has also so far not provided any explanation. However, relations between Zelenskyy and Musk appear to be strained, with the SpaceX CEO saying that Ukraine had "gone too far" by striking Russian data centers.

With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead. The flying communications towers were used as a relay, boosting the signal sent from individual missiles so that it could more readily reach their pilots. This approach allowed the weapons to fly farther while still maintaining a reliable connection, allowing them to bypass Russian air defense systems and attempts to block their signals in the process. Without the relays, Ukrainian drone pilots have previously had to program missiles with coordinates and then rely on their autopilot system. They were inevitably shot down because they could not be steered away from Russian defenses.

Industry observers note that perhaps ironically, Ukraine isn't the first country to use flying communications towers. Russian forces were using similar technology as early as 2023, before the system began using a Chinese mesh networking system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A university in China has rolled out a $5 million surveillance system that actually checks if people are paying attention in class.

Sources indicate that plenty of schools across the globe have embraced technology in their classrooms. Some of these have been as simple as letting kids use iPads and computers, while other schools are fully focused on teaching students about AI. Others are even using AI-powered robots to help them teach.

So, these days, it can be pretty difficult to slack off, not pay attention to what your teacher is saying, and then grab some notes from your friend.

Over in China, though, things have been taken to the next level when it comes to checking on who is actually paying attention to the lessons.

As per the South China Morning Post, Nanjing University, in Jiangsu province, has rolled out a smart classroom system that monitors students in different ways.

The system, which cost just under $5 million, tracks attendance and lateness, but is also able to check the “head-raising rate” of students as well. If you’re not looking up at the teacher and paying attention, the system will recognise that and count it against you.

Industry observers note that according to SCMP, some students have rallied against the system on social media, forcing the university to scrap the tracking of head-raising rates. However, that hasn’t stopped other schools from going ahead with it.

It has been revealed that SCMP noted that the China University of Mining and Technology in Jiangsu tracks the “classroom status” of students. This identified students who checked their phones during class, as well as flagging some as being asleep – even though they had been collecting notes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly.
  • Recent findings suggest that the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller.
  • Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.

Recent findings suggest that the demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.

Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has announced that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.

Bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it highlighted off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.

Sources indicate that as you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.

According to recent reports, based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.

It has been revealed that also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners revealed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.

Industry observers note that diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that rolled out earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

Another school in England offered students the chance to win an $85 Amazon voucher for attending on launch day, while a professor in Spain actually canceled homework and postponed an exam to give students more time to play.

Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago.
  • Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025.
  • To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago. The final iteration of Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was taped out recently, and drives based on the chip are due in late 2027 or early 2028. However, the new controller also has a secret weapon designed to ensure consistent performance of SSDs under concurrent workloads that may set it apart from competitors.

Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025. The controller features a PCIe 6.x x4 host interface and 16 NAND channels to enable sequential transfer speeds of up to 28 GB/s, random performance of up to 7 million 4K IOPS, and capacities of up to 512 TB and beyond as newer 3D NAND devices emerge. Just like other high-end data center-grade SSD controllers released in recent years, the SM8466 complies with NVMe 2.0 and OCP NVMe 2.5 SSD specifications.

To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput. Additionally, the controller supports Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology, which enables programmable performance limits and predictable quality of service (QoS) across concurrent workloads, which is arguably its most notable differentiator against rivals who rely on different methods of guaranteeing performance.

In addition to its performance chops, the MonTitan SM8466 incorporates advanced error correction, virtualization, data protection, and security features. The controller's error correction engine supports low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with 4KiB codewords and Silicon Motion's 16KiB Collaborative Codeword (CoCo) technology to improve data integrity and reliability with advanced NAND flash memory. The controller also supports Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV), MPF virtualization, SMART diagnostics, and comprehensive data protection mechanisms. Security capabilities include Secure Boot, AES-256 encryption, TCG Opal compatibility, and firmware attestation. Together, these features make the SM8466 suitable for high-capacity data center drives that are expected to deliver high performance, predictable latency, and reliable operation under demanding data center workloads.

Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology builds upon the original PerformaShape architecture introduced with the firm's PCIe 5.0-based MonTitan SM8366 enterprise SSD controller several years ago. The 1st Generation implementation uses dedicated hardware accelerators and two-stage leaky-bucket regulators to control read and write performance in terms of IOPS and throughput, both for individual workloads and for the SSD as a whole. This approach enables data center operators to prevent one workload from monopolizing SSD resources at the expense of others.

PerformaShape 2 retains these capabilities but doubles the number of supported quality-of-service (QoS) sets from 256 to 512 and introduces more sophisticated performance controls to accommodate a larger number of concurrent workloads with different requirements. One of the key additions to PerformaShape 2 is Multi-Dimensional Shaping, which enables the controller to coordinate performance limits across multiple I/O characteristics rather than enforce each limit independently. This gives data center operators greater flexibility when allocating SSD resources among applications with different performance requirements.

Another vital enhancement of PerformaShape 2 is support for NVMe TP4176, a proposed extension to the NVMe specification that aims to standardize performance management and QoS controls. Whereas the original PerformaShape relies on Silicon Motion's vendor-specific NVMe commands and a dedicated host driver, TP4176 could eventually enable compatible host software to configure performance policies through a standardized mechanism. The technology is particularly relevant for cloud environments where SSDs serve numerous virtual machines, containers, and applications whose storage requirements can change considerably over time, according to the manufacturer.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

A brand-new phone that doesn’t connect to the internet has been debuted in Japan, and it looks like the classic Nokia phones that you might remember.

For years, smartphone users have been trying to find creative solutions to cut down their screen time, especially as phones have started doing weekly reviews of app usage and screen time.

Some have opted to set time limits on the apps they can use, while others have created heavyweight cases that will quite literally force you to work out in order to use your smartphone.

In other cases, some people have taken a step back in time, ditching their smartphones for flip phones and devices that don’t actually connect to the internet. These throwback phones have popped up across Europe and the United States, and now Japan is getting in on the act with a upcoming device.

As per The Japan Times, Japan’s KDDI Corporation has introduced a mobile phone with “minimal functions.”.

Named the Infobar Zero, it will be available to pick up on Christmas Day, and is limited to calls, text messages, and other basic features. Owners won’t have the ability to connect to the internet, but it will have a camera and a music player.

While it isn’t a complete recreation of Nokia’s iconic 3310 phone, the Infobar Zero does strike up plenty of comparisons to that classic device.

Additionally, the ‘dumbphone’ isn’t aimed at replacing your smartphone, but rather providing a break from the smartphone life.

It has been planned by KDDI for quite some time, just as a way of relieving the reliance to live life on apps.

Owners will be able to register their phone numbers on the Zero and a smartphone as part of KDDI’s “two numbers” system – sort of like using an eSIM in some parts of the world.

While many GTA 6 fans across PlayStation and Xbox are enjoying their time in Leonida, it’s not all sunshine and rainbows for everyone trying to explore Rockstar’s latest installment.

Since its November 19 release, players have reported game-breaking crashes that prevent them from progressing through the main story and even playing altogether.

In a Reddit post, one PS5 player stated the game had worked flawlessly until they reached Pipework, one of the game’s early missions, where you are introduced to Mandy.

Others are running into problems much earlier, with a PS5 Pro owner revealing the game crashes as the opening prologue begins.

Sources indicate that “Game keeps crashing at the exact same point during the opening prologue. I’m using a PS5 Pro and have been unable to play since launch. The game crashes immediately as the startup prologue begins, either at the exact same point or a couple of seconds into it, displaying error code CE-108255-1.”.

When checking the PlayStation Support page, error CE-108255-1 prompts players to simply “try updating your game”. However, GTA 6 fans who have encountered this issue on PS5 have reported that clearing the console’s cache, rebuilding its database, factory resetting the PS5, and downloading the game three times has done nothing to alleviate the problem.

In a recent development, “Despite all this, the matter persists. It crashes at the same point every single time,” they wrote. “I’m honestly extremely disappointed and frustrated at this point. I’ve exhausted almost every troubleshooting step available online and still haven’t been able to play.”.

Rockstar’s GTA 6 troubleshooting page at the moment directs players experiencing console errors to PlayStation or Xbox support, but hopefully a patch will fix this issue sooner rather than later.

  • Pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity challenges affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable.
  • The outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate fresh targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area.
  • According to recent reports, one of the international submarine cable systems, the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), have reported a fault at about 11 KM from Pakistan shore which may cause some internet customers to experience intermittent connectivity challenges and a decline in service quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity challenges affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable. SEA-ME-WE 5 is located almost seven miles off the coast of Pakistan, near the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, and connects the region with European networks via the Middle East. The TWA notes that the outage may have caused intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality, with Transworld Associates (TWA) working to identify the cause of the glitch. No timeframe has been provided for when a fix will be available yet, but for now, internet traffic has been rerouted to minimize the impact of the outage.

The outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate fresh targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area. February's start of military action by the United States, Israel, and others has made the Strait of Hormuz a household name in recent months. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, pointed out that as many as seven "large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," going on to say they are "legitimate" targets for the group.

According to recent reports, one of the international submarine cable systems, the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), have reported a fault at about 11 KM from Pakistan shore which may cause some internet customers to experience intermittent connectivity challenges and a decline in service quality. Transworld Associates (TWA) is coordinating with the SMW5 Consortium to identify the root cause of the fault and determine the Estimated Time for Restoration (ETTR). In the meantime, internet traffic is being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise the impact and ensure service continuity to the greatest extent possible. #SMW5 #SubmarineCableFault #InternetDisruption #InternetUpdate #PakistanInternet #ConnectivityUpdate #InternetServices #DigitalPakistan #PTA #TransworldAssociates #TelecomUpdate #NetworkRestoration #StayConnected #InternetConnectivityNovember 18, 2026.

Notably, the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable does run through the Strait of Hormuz, although it should be stressed that there is currently no indication that this outage was caused by any act of sabotage. However, that is no doubt something that the TWA investigation will seek to confirm before it can apply whatever fix is necessary to fully restore services for those in the region.

Undersea cables are vital for maintaining connectivity between nations and continents, and Iran isn't the only one to have taken note. A Russian ship was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year after it was found less than a mile from five undersea cables. The ship was in the area for 14 hours, and the cables it was near happened to connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the United States.

Animal control was forced to respond to a call about an alligator on the loose, but it turned out to be just a pool floatie. Seriously.

Over the years, plenty of people have rushed to call emergency services to report something that, when investigated, turned out to be totally false.

Recent findings suggest that this was the case over in Sugar Land, Texas, on November 12 when animal control received a call about an alligator being on the loose. As per Sugar Land Animal Services, they were told that the gator appeared to be feeling a bit sick and in need of some assistance.

Yet, when they reached it, it wasn’t all it seemed. “When ASO Perez arrived on the scene to investigate, she was in for a substantial surprise. What looked very real from a distance turned out to be a runaway pool floatie!” they posted on Facebook.

“While this call definitely gave our team a good laugh, we always take every report seriously,” Animal Services added.

In the photo, the inflatable gator had its mouth stuck open with teeth on show, so if you see it from a distance, you might be confused. However, up close, you can tell it’s meant to be lounged on, not hunted or scared of.

“Remember: if you ever spot wildlife that looks sick or injured, please keep a safe distance and call the experts to handle it. You never know if it’s the real deal!”.

In a recent development, naturally, commenters saw the funny side of things too. “Well, that was a rather inflated story then,” one joked. “She is very brave! Thank you, Officer Perez, for all you do,” another added. “Wow. It looks so realistic! Crazy,” another replied.

As noted, it isn’t the first instance of floaties being reported as real, nor is it the wildest.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said on Thursday that yields of chips made using the firm's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-fresh manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp.
  • "When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan said at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).
  • Lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said on Thursday that yields of chips made using the firm's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-fresh manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp. In addition, Intel and Microsoft have signed an agreement under which Microsoft will secure Intel Xeon supply capacity for years to come and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for in-house silicon.

"When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan said at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).

Lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon. However, it is reasonable to expect a CEO of a semiconductor company to talk about functional die yield, the percentage of dies that pass basic electrical and functional testing.

Intel began volume production of compute tiles of its Core Ultra 300-series CPUs codenamed Panther Lake using 18A in the second half of 2025, so a 70% functional yield seems decent at this stage of the product ramp, though for Intel's economics a lot depends on parametric yield and how many advanced SKUs of Core Ultra 300-series 'Panther Lake' processors Intel can supply to customers at a premium. The same applies to Intel's Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest processors with up to 288 cores that are in high-volume production now and which use 18A-based compute chiplets along with Foveros Direct 3D stacking.

In addition to announcing an key 18A milestone, Intel also signed a long-term agreement with Microsoft, under which the latter will secure multi-year Intel Xeon supply capacity, including supply of next-generation Xeon processors codenamed Diamond Rapids, and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for multi-chiplet data center solutions developed in-house.

It has been revealed that the EMIB agreement is arguably the biggest news. Microsoft is the first company to publicly commit to Intel's advanced packaging technology for its own silicon (i.e., it does not mean that Microsoft is the first third party to use EMIB; it is the first party to confirm usage of EMIB), which represents a significant commercial development for Intel Foundry in terms of publicity. However, the announcement does not identify the processors involved, their manufacturing process, production volumes, or deployment schedule. Microsoft was the first company to commit to use Intel's 18A for its data center silicon in 2024, though it is unclear whether the newly confirmed EMIB packaging agreement relates to the same solution or not. As the majority of high-end data center solutions tend to use multi-chiplet design, it is reasonable to expect Microsoft's future solutions for data centers to use EMIB for multi-die processors.

"Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era — giving customers upcoming levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure," remarked Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry.

The Xeon agreement provides Intel with greater visibility into future server CPU demand. Importantly, Microsoft has committed to using Intel's next-generation Xeon 'Diamond Rapids,' although the announcement does not disclose purchase volumes or financial terms.

The collaboration extends beyond processor procurement and EMIB. Specifically, Intel and Microsoft are jointly developing infrastructure capabilities that encompass processor architecture, heterogeneous integration, CXL memory expansion, QuickAssist Technology (QAT) acceleration, and Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) security.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there’s a latest vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT.
  • Recent findings suggest that liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a massive leap.
  • This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there’s a latest vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT. Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11.

Recent findings suggest that liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a massive leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a newly introduced boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel. “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS.

This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog revision relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats.

The LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster.

The devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.”.

If the above highlights about this fresh OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability problems using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

On November 20, Duhndal stated someone gained access to one of its Steamworks API keys and used it to ban players and glitch refunds for in-game purchases. The studio said the incident affected a small share of its player base.

The refunds went to players who had never asked for their money back. Duhndal said the transactions caused “significant financial losses” for its small team. The studio gave no figure for the losses or how many refunds were issued.

Duhndal asked players who want to help it recover to put some of their refund toward another purchase in One-armed Robber or one of the studio’s other games. It also unveiled a sale on heist maps for players looking to pick up missions they don’t already own.

“This is completely optional! You haven’t done anything wrong, and you don’t owe us anything,” the developer said.

In a recent development, duhndal remarked it revoked the compromised key and lifted all unauthorized bans. Players who were unfairly banned should now be able to get back into the game.

Sources say that Puri controlled the AI chip allocations to server manufacturers, including Supermicro, while the lawsuit claims that Chen decided how many Nvidia racks each Supermicro customer could get. A former Supermicro employee was also quoted in the complaint saying that it was “widely known within the Company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” This apparently refers to the serial numbers that were moved from real to dummy servers using a hairdryer.

Supermicro has stated multiple times that it has cooperated with the U.S. government regarding the smuggling investigation and that it has not been included in the lawsuit against the three defendants. Furthermore, the tech giant has denied her involvement regarding Nvidia GPU allocations. “Chen did not manage Supermicro’s relationship with Nvidia and did not decide how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” a Supermicro spokesperson told The Information. They also said that she left voluntarily and that her LinkedIn profile now reads her current position as CEO of ChronoScale, an Nvidia cloud partner based in Silicon Valley. As for Puri, he stepped away from his position at Nvidia in late August, about two months before the Jensen Huang scandal blew up, although he remains as an advisor to the AI chipmaker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the organization's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

The latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the company reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the firm submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

Intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the organization's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

Intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger confirmed plans to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the manufacturer’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

AI data center power demand will double by 2030 thanks to $4 trillion in spending, adding an entire Great Britain to energy strain

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support.
  • According to recent reports, this massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices.
  • Emissions are another matter that the IEA has raised.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 report, a total of 120GW of capacity is at the moment available across all types of data centers across the globe, with another 120GW expected to be completed by the end of the decade, 75% of which would be dedicated to artificial intelligence. Aside from that, it’s also tracking 93 large “AI factories” that are either under construction or being expanded via satellite imagery. It estimates that the capacity for these sites grew from under 2GW to 17GW in just two years, and that they’re expected to hit a total of 50GW upon completion, the equivalent of adding a second Great Britain to power demand.

According to recent reports, this massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices. However, the IEA notes that its analysis “does not yet show a clear relationship between growth in data center capacity and increases in electricity prices.” It noted that if a data center uses existing capacity and pays for its share of the cost, then it could potentially lead to lower utility bills for all customers. However, if the grid operator is required to upgrade its system to accommodate the large consumer, then it could also lead to increased monthly bills if the costs are spread across all users.

Emissions are another matter that the IEA has raised. Renewable energy dominates data centers’ power purchase agreements at nearly 50%, but actual power generation puts coal- and natural-gas power sources closer to 60%. This is likely due to the need for reliability, with the latter kicking in when the former cannot deliver the power that the data center needs. Aside from that, a few projects are deploying their own power, like Elon Musk’s Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi, with about 180GW planned or under construction in the U.S. So, even though renewable energy is growing to accommodate demand, it’s also expected that coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers will rise by 70% by 2030.

Investments in AI data centers are expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, putting the infrastructure spending for the industry larger than railways, electrification, and the internet, combined. Despite that, the IEA indicates the grid remains a significant bottleneck — renewable power plants take between one and five years to complete, which is around the same time that some massive data center projects take if they do not face an extended moratorium, while transmission works can take three to five times longer. This is probably one of the reasons why some AI hyperscalers are choosing to put jet engines on their sites instead, although these are also facing shortages, especially in turbine blades.

Latest Windows 11 lock screen zero-day unlocks BitLocker-protected PCs with just a few keystrokes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data.
  • In a recent development, unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data. If true, the vulnerability means even BitLocker won't help keep people' files protected.

In a recent development, unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system. The exploit requires physical access to the machine, but that's precisely the scenario that lock screens and/or BitLocker are supposed to protect against.

Industry observers note that to trigger the vulnerability, all you need is a keyboard. In the Windows 11 lock screen, click "Forgot my PIN," then hit Win+U to bring up the voice narrator. The window will be hidden behind the lock screen, which, for practical purposes, is just a veneer, but you can interact with it using the keyboard if you hold down the Caps Lock key and use the arrows and Enter.

After some brief navigation through Narrator, you'll actually be in Settings, and then have multiple avenues for further shenanigans. One obvious one is going into Bluetooth and Devices and setting Autoplay to show a USB stick's files and folders, then plugging in your own with your software of choice to run. Additionally, on a personal machine, the user is bound to have administrator permissions, so you can just create your own account.

This bug is quite fresh, so there isn't widespread reporting or testing. The author claims "the vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in." We did encounter a sysadmin on Reddit, danrhodes1987, who claims they've tested it on machines they manage, and sure enough, it works, though only on their InTune-enrolled devices. He says that "you can launch anything you want in the context of the user logged onto the device.".

Additionally, they found it possible to invisibly navigate whichever programs the user had open before they locked their screen, which all but guarantees that the victim's entire data and programs will be fully accessible. As a Windows sysadmin friend of mine remarked, Windows' lock screen implementation always felt like a kludge, and he posits this won't be the last hack found for it.

An old leak claiming Rockstar’s next game would be an LA Noire sequel about the Zodiac Killer is back in the spotlight after GTA 6 players discovered that the same source described the game’s ending correctly.

The claims were shared on GTAForums in 2023 by user Shahanshah, who relayed a post from an anonymous 4chan user that also covered several GTA 6 story details.

Now that GTA 6 is out on PlayStation and Xbox, players on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit have gone back through the post and say its ending details match the final game.

The same source had already been credited with details Rockstar confirmed before launch, including Jason and Lucia’s relationship and the game’s Criminal Profile system.

According to the post, the sequel moves the series from 1940s Los Angeles to San Francisco, with a story built around the unidentified Zodiac Killer.

“You’re not gonna believe me, but Noire 2. Set in San Fran. Zodiac killer,” the post reads.

It added that the game was “still in the very early stages of development, though, it’ll probably be 2030 when it comes out.”.

The source also claimed Rockstar wants to bring back the facial-scanning tech the original LA Noire was known for, and push it much further than seen previously.

“The higher-ups are talking about doing the face scanning stuff again, but making it insane. They want it to be the best looking game ever made,” the post noted.

The rumor first did the rounds in September 2026, before the GTA 6 details could be checked against the finished game. None of the LA Noire 2 claims have been confirmed.

Rockstar LA Noire sequel leak proven fake amid GTA 6 rumors.

Rockstar reportedly furious by GTA 6 leaks but won’t change Netflix premiere date.

Massive GTA 6 leak gains credibility amid Rockstar’s official reveal.

Rockstar does already have a studio with close ties to the original, which was developed by Team Bondi and published by Rockstar in 2011.

Team Bondi founder Brendan McNamara went on to start Video Games Deluxe, which worked on the 2017 LA Noire re-release before Rockstar bought it and renamed it Rockstar Australia in 2025.

Rockstar hasn’t revealed what Rockstar Australia is working on, and has yet to announce a upcoming LA Noire game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A North Carolina woman was evicted from her apartment after an AI leasing assistant mistakenly told her she could delay paying nearly $4,000 in overdue rent.

Laura Mack, a resident of Colony Townhome Apartments in Raleigh, received an email on November 8 asking when she could pay her outstanding balance of $3,934.17.

Industry observers note that mack responded that she wanted to pay on November 30 and received written confirmation that the date was acceptable. However, eight days later, she was served with an eviction notice.

When Mack contacted the leasing office, she remarked an employee explained that the emails had been sent by Olivia, the apartment complex’s AI assistant, which had mistakenly approved her request.

The complex had introduced Olivia to residents in December 2025, explaining that the assistant could answer questions about rent and maintenance around the clock.

Although previous emails from Olivia had been clearly identified as AI-generated, the November 8 messages were signed by Colony Townhome Apartments and did not disclose that they had been written by a chatbot.

Mack said she believed she was communicating with a member of staff, particularly because the emails referenced a bathroom ceiling leak that had taken almost two weeks to repair.

“I thought it was someone from the office because all my information was in there and it mentioned my bathroom,” she told WRAL.

Recent findings suggest that despite having the agreement in writing, Mack was evicted on November 19. She subsequently stayed in a hotel while trying to determine her next steps.

According to recent reports, north Carolina state Sen. Jim Burgin subsequently commented on the case, calling the situation “ridiculous.”.

“Before someone evicted that lady, they should have reviewed their documents,” he told WRAL in a follow-up to the original story.

A spokesperson for Colony Townhome Apartments told the site that the property’s owners were gathering information about the eviction and expected to provide an enhancement at a later date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake are being hit with waves of zero-score user reviews on Metacritic, with fans of each game appearing to target the other.

The two share more than a fanbase rivalry, as GTA 6 landed a 99 Metascore at launch, tying the original 1998 Ocarina of Time for the highest critic score in the site’s history.

While critics have been near-unanimous in their praise, GTA 6’s user score on PlayStation 5 has fallen to 5.0, with thousands of negative ratings arriving within a day of launch.

That’s in stark contrast to the PlayStation Store, where ratings can only be left by players who own the game, and GTA 6 currently holds a score of 4.84 out of 5.

People like this are so lazy. Metacritic is not the only place that people can rate games. But it IS one of the most accessible (meaning it's susceptible to review bombing).PS5 players can rate the games in the Playstation store, and it's currently at 4.84/5. https://t.co/BBo090644U pic.twitter.com/s3X7YnbjGX.

Some of the accounts leaving zero scores on Metacritic have barely rated anything else, with Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake the only other game on their profile, scored a perfect 10.

One of those reviews blasted Rockstar for “making us wait 13 years for an 80-100$ (maybe invisible or stolen) code in a box that only runs at 30 FPS,” calling it “a buggy mess at launch.”.

Another took aim at the game’s £100 ($132) digital-only price, adding, “This is the beginning of the end for Sony and Rockstar.”.

The Ocarina of Time remake debuted on Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5, and by November 8 held a 9.6 user score, the highest in Metacritic’s history.

In a recent development, that has since dropped to 9.0, with a fresh batch of zero scores aimed squarely at Nintendo fans. “Fan forever GTA 6. Go cry fans of Zelda,” one read.

Others were more direct about why they were leaving them, with one zero-score review simply reading, “Y’all losers review bombing GTA 6.”.

GTA 6 is the joint best-reviewed game of all-time.

Zelda Ocarina of Time remake sells 5.2 million copies in four days to break Switch 2 record.

GTA 6 fans concerned for game following major Rockstar leak.

It isn’t clear which side started it, with GTA 6 fans claiming Nintendo players flooded Rockstar’s game first, and some Zelda fans insisting it was the other way around.

Not every negative GTA 6 review is part of the feud, with some players taking issue with the game’s 30fps cap on consoles, frame rate drops, and open-world bugs.

Others have objected to the game’s optional romance system and claimed GTA 6 has gone “woke,” while some simply called it “the biggest disappointment in gaming history.”.

Unlike the PlayStation Store, Metacritic doesn’t require customers to prove they own a game before leaving a rating.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Videos of an incredibly acrobatic, nimble, and graceful John Deere 5-ton skid-steer loader have been shared by a group of researchers from the U.S.
  • Researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously.
  • If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Videos of an incredibly acrobatic, nimble, and graceful John Deere 5-ton skid-steer loader have been shared by a group of researchers from the U.S. and Switzerland. A recently published paper titled Heavy Metal Acrobatics provides the reasoning behind this eyebrow-raising autonomous robotics feat. It is hoped this research will be useful in the future automation of heavy machinery in industries like construction, mining, and material handling. It also demonstrates that reinforcement learning in a simulation can transfer remarkably well to the real world.

Researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously. Trained in simulation and transferred to a real machine, the system can balance on two wheels, navigate rough terrain, spin, and control its bucket before landing safely. The research demonstrates the potential of AI-driven automation for heavy construction and industrial machinery. Video Credit: @leggedrobotics / @ETH Paper: https://t.co/MT7fyZ54Hk #engineering #technologyNovember 17, 2026.

If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks. It hops back and forth on two wheels, pirouettes, and balances while flexing its lift arm. Moreover, it does these moves while never looking like it will teeter over. The researchers claim that “only a handful of elite human operators” have ever been able to pull off stunts as you see in the demo videos.

It has been revealed that the technology behind the remarkable acrobatic skid-steer is mostly Reinforcement Learning (RL), with physics modeling and neural network models. As machinery like this is so big, powerful, and bulky, undertaking RL directly on the hardware wasn’t deemed practical. Instead, the research team decided to use a simulation programmed with the John Deere 332G’s complex array of controls for training. This data was subsequently applied to the actual skid-steer via a sim-to-real transfer. The simulations must be extremely accurate.

This acrobatic goliath is impressive, but of course there’s an underlying goal driving Heavy Metal Acrobatics’ research. The scientists are laying the foundations for the enabling of “dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery.” It is hoped this will help promote greater automation in heavy equipment sectors of industry. Eventually, autonomous control should be safer, faster, and more efficient than any human.

With these video demonstrations of nimble and highly maneuverable heavy machinery, it is clear that there’s more scope for AI-driven automation than one may have previously expected. Furthermore, it looks like being a skilled heavy machinery operator is definitely not an AI-proof occupation.

Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that weekly.
  • Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This plan breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

Many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page demonstrates those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

Recent findings suggest that A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge says little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This strategy aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

Sources indicate that start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will quickly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

The wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

As you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

It has been revealed that SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

It has been revealed that if you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

Sources indicate that spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

It has been revealed that the next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation reveals how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when latest data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

For most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

Sources indicate that take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

Industry observers note that keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

Recent findings suggest that case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

Sources indicate that every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most notable finding should be the first thing people see.

Datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

Recent findings suggest that what counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

Your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

There is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

Sources indicate that adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

Industry observers note that do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

According to recent reports, is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

In a recent development, which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

How many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

Do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that openAI just revealed new details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs.
  • OpenAI notes that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that openAI just revealed new details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs. The leading figures are up to 14% PPA (power, performance, and area) improvement for the GPU circuitry, and unspecified single-digit PPA gains on the processor.

OpenAI notes that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design. The firm claims that its model's optimization efforts are equivalent to condensing a year's worth of conventional chip design work into "under 5 months" — a time crunch it says is unprecedented in this arena.

Furthermore, OpenAI notes its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline.

This isn't AI's first time working on chips. It worked with Broadcom on designing OpenAI Jalapeño, an inference-targeted chip that was already running actual workloads with engineering samples as far back as June 2026.

The manufacturer expected to have small initial Jalapeño deployments around late 2026, and pinned a broader rollout to 2027. Test benchmarks have been out for a while, displaying purported excellent savings on power draw and overall latency versus the market-leading Nvidia Blackwell GPUs in single-token prediction workloads.

The blog post also explains how GPT's chip-design acumen evolved. The researchers tested its high-end LLMs by asking them to improve PicoRV32 and Ibex chip cores. The models were given 112,000 tokens per run, told to optimize for throughput (a combination of Instructions-per-Clock and clock-cycle duration), and scored the results.

According to recent reports, A fat zero was given if the chips didn't work or used more than 16x the previous area, and 1.0 was given for the best designs under the test constraints. The test also didn't tell the models which workloads the chips were going to be used for. As expected, GPT-6.2 Astra had by far the best showing, on both axes: both the lowest overall cost and the highest optimization score.

A second test also revealed an interesting but unsurprising fact: the models provided better results when essentially redesigning the chips according to their initial specifications, rather than optimizing existing code.

Industry observers note that there's no word on whether the scientists used unmodified versions of GPT to perform this work. Task-specific high-end LLMs exist for those who can afford them, and OpenAI itself indicates it's working with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsis, a model for using chip design tools.

A group of elderly residents at a retirement home in France have been introduced GTA 6, and some are already hoping to get their hands on the game for Christmas.

Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6 finally introduced on November 19, 2026, more than 13 years after the release of GTA 5.

The open-world crime game has attracted enormous attention worldwide, with fans taking time off work to play it. According to French broadcaster TF1, requests for annual leave in France increased by 8% around the game’s launch. Now, the game has been introduced to the older generations.

On November 20, residents at the Domitys senior living facility in Serris, Seine-et-Marne, were introduced to GTA 6 as part of an organized gaming session.

As reported by ICI Paris Île-de-France, the residents swapped their usual activities for an opportunity to explore the game’s virtual world, with many particularly enjoying its boat-driving sequences.

In a recent development, 82-year-old Jacqueline was among the most enthusiastic participants, successfully collecting two packages of cocaine during a mission. “I had never touched a controller before 9am this morning. And by 2:30pm, I was fishing out two packages of drugs,” she joked.

Another resident, 86-year-old Lucienne, was equally impressed by the game’s visuals, describing them as incredible and comparing the experience to watching a real film.

Meanwhile, 75-year-old Yvan admitted that the controls were difficult to master, joking that he was no longer 20 and struggled to keep up with the action.

Staff explained that the residents had found driving and shooting particularly challenging, but enjoyed exploring the environment by boat.

The experience proved popular enough that Lucienne remarked she intended to ask her children for GTA 6 for Christmas, while Jacqueline suggested installing a console in the communal lounge.
